overview.text: A base is best understood by what it does in a reaction: in Brønsted–Lowry chemistry, it accepts a proton (H⁺) from an acid. That definition is broader than treating every base as a substance containing hydroxide; for example, ammonia accepts a proton from water and forms ammonium, while water becomes hydroxide. In water at 25 °C, a basic solution has pH above 7 and more hydroxide than hydronium ions; neutral water is pH 7 at that temperature. Bases matter because they can reduce acidity through neutralization. Bases also differ in strength: strong bases form hydroxide extensively in water, while weak bases react only partly. A compound’s base behavior depends on the reaction and solvent.

key_facts.text: A Brønsted–Lowry base accepts a proton; after accepting it, the base becomes its conjugate acid.
Ammonia is a base even though it contains no hydroxide: in water, it accepts a proton and forms ammonium and hydroxide ions.
At 25 °C, aqueous solutions with pH above 7 are basic; the pH boundary depends on temperature, so pH 7 is not a universal definition of a base.
In water, strong bases produce hydroxide extensively, while weak bases react only partly; strength describes reaction extent, not simply how concentrated a solution is.
Adding a base to an acidic solution can lower its acidity and move it toward neutral; this process is called neutralization.
